name: SQL Injection Through AI
title: SQL Injection Through AI
answer: SQL injection is the insertion of malicious query text into a database command. When an AI system generates SQL from user or document input, prompt injection can produce harmful queries. Generated SQL therefore needs the same controls as any untrusted input, including least privilege, read only access where possible, and query review. The scope covers text to SQL features, AI agents that call database tools, and any pipeline where model output becomes executable SQL.

sections.body: SQL injection is the insertion of malicious query text into a database command. When an AI system generates SQL from user or document input, prompt injection can produce harmful queries. Generated SQL therefore needs the same controls as any untrusted input, including least privilege, read only access where possible, and query review. The scope covers text to SQL features, AI agents that call database tools, and any pipeline where model output becomes executable SQL.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large language models, agent frameworks, and tool calling layers that connect to relational databases and warehouses. This site tracks 263 Model Context Protocol servers for SQL databases and warehouses, which is one sign of how common that connection has become. The databases themselves are often PostgreSQL, MySQL, or cloud warehouses, and the site's own pages are built from a PostgreSQL database. Execution usually happens through a database driver or API with a service account, so the model never touches the database directly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical flow starts with a user prompt, a document, or a chat message that is combined into a model request. The model returns SQL text, which an application extracts, sometimes with a parser or a regular expression, and then sends to the database. Prompt injection can change that SQL by adding conditions, unions, stacked statements, or calls to sensitive functions. Teams test for this with red team prompts, fuzzing, and static checks on generated queries, then compare the result against an expected query shape.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because generated SQL can be traced back to a prompt, a model version, a tool call, and a database role. Logs often record the original input, the generated query, the user or service identity, and the rows or objects affected. Risk includes data exfiltration, unintended writes, privilege escalation, and compliance exposure when sensitive tables are reachable. Access reviews, read only roles, and audit trails are common controls, and data protection rules may limit what can be sent to a model in the first place.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More AI agents are gaining database access through tool protocols, so the boundary between prompt injection and SQL injection will keep blurring. Expect more SQL aware guardrails, policy engines, and query firewalls that inspect generated statements before execution. Provenance standards and evaluation suites for text to SQL security are likely to mature, alongside research on detecting harmful queries. The long term direction is to treat model output as untrusted input at every step, from prompt to row.
